For polyglot data science, RStudio is too specific, VS Code is too general, but Positron is just right. However, it’s not without friction. With two years of experience teaching Python with Positron, I’ll discuss how Positron fits in the data stack and how it helps address the “three bears” of teaching Python. 

Positron has recently been made available on [JupyterHub](https://positron.posit.co/blog/posts/2026-04-03-positron-server-jupyterhub/), which is a great place to start, but I think students need to be able to wean themselves off of web-based tools and learn how to manage local installations so that they can take it with them after graduation and be prepared for similar setups in practice.

## Introduction

Nearly two years ago, [Positron](https://posit.co/products/ide/positron/), Posit's "next-generation data science IDE," was revealed. As a long-time [RStudio](https://posit.co/products/open-source/rstudio/) user and teacher who was preparing to teach in Python for the first time, I was intrigued. A [week after the reveal](https://occasionaldivergences.com/posts/positron-intro/), I wrote:

> If RStudio is too specific and VS Code is too general, is Positron just right? Again, your mileage may vary, and it is still in beta, but having some of the core features of RStudio made available for a polyglot, VS Code-based data science IDE is *compelling*. With Positron it really looks like we might be able to get the best of both worlds.

After nearly two years, with Positron well out of beta, I think we are getting the best of both worlds. And after more than a year of teaching in Python, I also think that Positron is just right for teaching data science. However, this isn't without some friction, most of which relates to students readiness to code locally.

![](figures/just-right.png){width=50% fig-align="center"}

This post is for anyone who is curious about using Positron for teaching data science. I'll share what I've done, what's worked well, and where I hope to improve and see less friction for students.

## Positron in the data stack

I am an assistant professor in the Data Analytics and Information Systems Department at the [Jon M. Huntsman School of Business](https://huntsman.usu.edu) at Utah State University where I both teach and research along with working as a faculty mentor in the [Analytics Solutions Center](https://huntsman.usu.edu/asc/). I recommend students use Positron and demonstrate its use in both classroom and mentorship settings. The students I teach and mentor are typically upper-class undergraduates and master's students who have had some previous coursework or experience coding in Python before I work with them.

In their prior coursework or experience, my students almost universally have experience coding using Jupyter notebooks and Google Colab. Many of them have tried using another code editor or IDE, typically VS Code or some forked variant. I recommend that my students and mentees use Positron as part of a specific [data stack](https://github.com/marcdotson/data-stack), with thanks to Emily Riederer’s blog series beginning with [Python Rgonomics](https://emilyriederer.netlify.app/post/py-rgo-2025/), which includes:

- Python for data wrangling, visualizations, and modeling
- Positron as the integrated development environment (IDE)
- GitHub for version control, project management, and collaboration
- Quarto for communicating results with presentations, reports, dashboards, etc.
- Copilot for assisting with code development and data analysis

Python is required for students in my program and all students at Utah State at least have access to Copilot.

## Where Positron is just right

While not all students opt to use Positron as part of the recommended data stack, many do. Positron is just right in the ways that any Positron user would expect. Support for data science tasks and the inclusion of features like the data explorer, variables pane, and plots pane out-of-the-box are an immediate win. In fact, the features are so helpful and intuitive that students typically don't fully appreciate how much friction has been so effortlessly handled for them. This is Hadley Wickham's "pit of success" writ large.

A related area where Positron is just right is how it can help students move on from Jupyter notebooks. Again, my students almost universally have experience coding using Jupyter notebooks---but many of them have never done anything *but* code in Jupyter notebooks. It can be a challenge for them to understand basic coding tasks like code execution without a cell. However, it is also an opportunity for them to understand coding without the crutch of a notebook and to consider how code can produce other outputs.

## Where students experience friction

Students experience friction in the ways that any Python user would expect. Installing Python and managing virtual environments are always a challenge, though [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) in particular has helped massively on this front and has been embraced by the Positron development team and included in the built-in project environment tooling. Of course, cloud-based environments like Google Colab and Posit Cloud can help reduce this friction, but students need to face it at some point as they prepare to work across a variety of coding environments in practice.

To be fair, students experience this friction whether or not they opt to use Positron. I think it's telling of how well Positron works that it's these long-existing challenges that exist around the use of the IDE that cause friction for students, not using the IDE itself.

## Final thoughts

In my polyglot experience, RStudio is too specific and VS Code is too general---but Positron is just right, including for teaching data science. I'm hopeful that Positron and Quarto together can help cure student reliance on notebooks, this generation's "death by PowerPoint," and that tooling in and around Positron will continue to reduce the friction of installing Python and managing virtual environments.
